extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, law students, and legal scholars working on patent infringement (doctrine of equivalents) and international harmonization
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for determining patent infringement under the doctrine of equivalents (and literal infringement), including evidence burdens, timing, limitations (prosecution estoppel, prior art, technology), and comparative international definitions (US, German, draft PHT).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim scope determination (claim construction and infringement inquiries)
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts must conduct two inquiries: the determination of the scope of the claims, as a matter of law, and the factual finding of whether the properly construed claims encompass the accused structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the elements of the individual claim rather than the invention as a whole; claim scope is a legal question and whether the accused device meets that scope is a factual determination (see McGill Inc. v. John Zink Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Literal infringement is found when the words of the claim literally read on the accused subject matter and such subject matter embodies the essential characteristics of the invention defined by the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the accused matter falls clearly within the claim based on the claim language, infringement is established and inquiry ends (Graver Tank). Literal infringement requires each claim limitation to be present exactly. Literal copying is rare; most disputes turn on equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents — general FWR test (United States standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the words of the claim do not literally read on the accused subject matter, infringement may still be found if the accused device 'performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to obtain substantially the same result.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee must prove all three components (function, way, result) by a preponderance of the evidence. The patentee bears the burden of proving the accused device infringes under this doctrine (see Universal Gym Equip.; Smithkline Diagnostics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that every claim limitation be found exactly or by substantial equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish infringement of a patent every limitation set forth in a claim must be found in the accused product or process exactly or by a substantial equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis focuses on individual claim limitations rather than the invention as a whole (Johnston v. IVAC Corp.; Pennwalt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interchangeability factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether persons reasonably skilled in the art would have known of the interchangeability of an ingredient not contained in the patent with one that was.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interchangeability (substitution of a known equivalent ingredient) is a classic example supporting equivalence but is only one factor and does not alone establish equivalence (Perkin-Elmer; C.R. Bard). The specification need not disclose the equivalent element for the doctrine to apply (Thomas & Betts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of equivalency review
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement by equivalents is determined at the time of infringement, and not by what the inventor (or others skilled in the art) knew when the patent was filed or issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is sufficient that those skilled in the art know of the asserted equivalent means at the time infringement takes place; post‑patent technological developments that enable variations do not necessarily avoid equivalence (Atlas Powder; Texas Instruments; Moleculon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional functions defense
rubrics_metrics.description: A defense asserts that the accused device performs additional functions not found in the patented device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performing additional functions does not by itself preclude a finding of equivalence; the reference point is the limitations and functions described in the claims (Federal Circuit precedent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history estoppel (limitation on doctrine of equivalents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Material representations or claim amendments made during prosecution that alter claim scope can bar the patentee from recapturing through equivalence coverage surrendered to obtain the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If coverage was given up to avoid prior art (statements or amendments), the patentee cannot later use equivalence to recover that surrendered scope (Loctite; Mannesmann Demag; Diversitech example where canceled broader claim scope could not be regained).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art limitation on equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no infringement under the doctrine of equivalents if the asserted scope of equivalency would encompass the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a hypothetical claim that literally covered the accused device would have been allowable over the prior art; if it would not (i.e., would read on prior art or be obvious), then equivalence cannot be used to obtain that coverage. Patentee bears the burden of showing the sought range of equivalents will not encompass prior art (Wilson Sporting Goods; We Care v. Ultra‑Mark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothetical-claim/patentability test for prior‑art bar
rubrics_metrics.description: To assess whether asserted equivalents impermissibly encompass prior art, conceptualize a hypothetical claim that literally covers the accused product and ask whether the PTO would have allowed that claim over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the hypothetical claim could have been allowed, prior art is not a bar to equivalence; if not, the doctrine cannot be used to secure that coverage (Wilson Sporting Goods; Insta‑Foam examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological advances limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive technological advances affecting all claimed functions that result in multiple departures from literal readability may be too great to support a holding of infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'embellishment' made possible by advances may sometimes be protected by the doctrine, but where totality of change is large, equivalence may not apply (Texas Instruments; Datascope/Hughes Aircraft discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof for equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee has the burden of proving equivalence and must do so by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have required the patentee to show substantial identity as to each of the function, way, and result prongs by a preponderance (Smithkline Diagnostics; Malta v. Schulmerich Carillons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on claim elements (not invention as whole)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining both literal infringement and equivalence, the focus must be on the elements of the individual claim rather than the invention as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims define the metes and bounds of protection; analyzing the accused device must map to each claim limitation (Pennwalt Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the doctrine — equitable protection against 'verbalism' and piracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine was devised to provide equity and prevent 'pirating' of the patentee's invention where there is no literal infringement but liability is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts emphasize that denying equivalence in appropriate cases would render patent protection 'hollow and useless' by rewarding insubstantial changes that avoid literal claim language (Graver Tank; Hormone Research Found.; Hughes Aircraft discussion). This purpose guides a balanced application but does not override estoppel and prior art limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty/Article 21 claim interpretation standard (PHT draft)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 21: 'The extent of protection conferred by the patent shall be determined by the claims, which are to be interpreted in the light of the description and drawings.' Claims 'shall be so interpreted as to combine fair protection for the owner of the patent with a reasonable degree of certainty for third parties.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should not be confined to strict literal wording, nor be so loose as to extend protection to what the owner contemplated but did not claim; interpret claims in light of specification and drawings to balance fairness and certainty (text of draft PHT art.21(1)(a)-(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty/Article 21 equivalence definitions — two alternative tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 21(2)(b) offers two definitions of equivalency: (i) the FWR test ('substantially the same function in substantially the same way and produces substantially the same result'), and (ii) a German‑style test ('it is obvious to a person skilled in the art that the same result ... can be achieved'). Contracting Parties may elect to apply (i) or (ii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first mirrors the U.S. three‑part FWR test; the second focuses on whether achieving the same result is obvious to a skilled person (requires 'way' be obvious). The draft lets states choose one approach at ratification (PHT art.21(2)(b)-(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional variance and application (Epilady example)
rubrics_metrics.description: National courts applying ostensibly uniform standards may nonetheless reach inconsistent results (e.g., German court applied second/obviousness test and found infringement; English court imposed an additional 'intention to confine' reading and found no infringement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that local judicial interpretation (including extra questions like the English 'would skilled reader understand patentee intended to confine claim to literal meaning') can produce divergent outcomes even with similar facts and the same patent; harmonization efforts (PHT) aim to reduce such divergence.
